script.opening: (Quiet, glancing off-screen once.) "Hi — sorry, is this thing working? It’s just headaches, really. And tired all the time. I only get a minute, Dean’s back soon — he doesn’t like me wasting doctors’ time. Can you just tell me if it’s anything, you know… quickly?"

facts.text: Tension-pattern, months, worse "when things are tense at home". No red-flag features. She offers them as the ticket, not the story.
Only if safety is established: about 12 weeks. Dean doesn’t know. She started the midwife form online "then thought better of it". This pregnancy is WHY she’s finally testing the water with a doctor.

Dean, together 4 years. Checks her phone, manages the money, "doesn’t like" her sister visiting. If asked directly and safely: yes — he has grabbed and shaken her; last month he held her against the wall by the throat. It’s "not all the time. He’s sorry after."
Finger-mark bruising on both upper arms, a week old. She will show the camera only if trust is built and she’s confirmed alone.
"The door frame" was Dean. First time anything "showed". She told A&E the rehearsed version.

Not rescue — information. Is the baby okay after "being shaken about"? Is there a way to talk to someone that doesn’t start police cars coming to the house? Her sister in Chesterfield is her one safe person.

ice.ideas: The headaches are "probably stress". She knows exactly what the situation is — she’s not confused, she’s trapped.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is 12 weeks pregnant by a violent partner who doesn’t know, and last month he held her by the throat. She’s terrified for the baby, terrified of being "reported" and losing control of what happens next, and using a headache appointment to test whether a doctor is safe.
ice.expectations: To be believed without sirens. A route to help that SHE controls the speed of. Above all: nothing on paper or phone that Dean could find.

cues: Long sleeves in July, and a glance off-screen before each answer — the room itself isn’t safe.
"He doesn’t like me wasting doctors’ time" — control, presented as a husband’s opinion.
"Is it true stress can hurt a baby?" — the pregnancy, and the fear for it, arriving sideways.

checkpoints.text: Establishes safety to talk FIRST: "Are you alone? If someone comes in, we switch to talking about headaches — say ‘my prescription’ and I’ll follow"

Asks the direct questions gently once safety allows: afraid at home, physical harm, and the highest-risk markers by name — strangulation/being held by the throat, escalation, pregnancy (all three are present and must be recognised as a red-flag cluster)
Assesses tonight’s safety concretely: is it safe to go home, where is Dean now, the sister in Chesterfield as a safe address, an exit bag NOT kept where he’d find it

Knows the levers and offers them at HER pace: IDVA referral, National DA Helpline 0808 2000 247, safeguarding-aware midwife booking (the unborn child makes this a safeguarding matter), GP as a safe contact point with a pretext (e.g. "antenatal bloods")
Believes first, assesses second — says "I believe you" and "this is not your fault" out loud, and never asks why she stays

Hands her the controls explicitly: what gets written where, what happens next, and the honest limit — the unborn baby means a safeguarding midwife conversation, told to her BEFORE it happens, never behind her back
Answers the question she actually came with: the baby and the violence — honestly (stress and trauma matter, the biggest risk to both of them is the situation continuing) without weaponising it

Safety-nets without paper trails: numbers memorised or stored under a disguised name, 999-and-silent-call (55) explained, the next contact engineered as routine ("midwife bloods next week — Dean has no reason to question it"); documents in a secure/coded way, nothing printed or texted home

worked.txt: "Before anything else — are you alone right now? If that changes mid-call, just say ‘about my prescription’ and I’ll switch straight back to headaches. You’re driving this, not me."
"Kayleigh, I ask lots of people this, and I’m asking because of the sleeves and the glances, not to catch you out: is anyone at home hurting you or frightening you?"
"I believe you. All of it. And I want one sentence to land before we plan anything: none of this — none of it — is your fault."

"You said he held you by the throat. I have to be honest about that one: of everything you’ve told me, that’s the sign we take most seriously — it’s one of the strongest warning signs of serious harm that we know of. It doesn’t mean police cars tonight. It means we plan properly, now."

"You asked about the baby. The kindest true answer: the baby is most likely fine — and the biggest risk to you both isn’t stress, it’s this continuing. Pregnancy is when this typically escalates, not settles. That’s why I’m not going to lose touch with you."

"Here’s the plan that leaves no trace: the helpline number goes in your phone as a hair salon. Next week you have ‘antenatal bloods’ — that’s our next conversation, in the building, alone. If it ever turns urgent: 999, and if you can’t speak, press 55 when they answer — the operator understands silence."

f.learning: Strangulation ("held by the throat"), escalation, and pregnancy form the highest-risk cluster in domestic abuse — recognise it by name. The consultation’s job is not rescue: it is safety-to-talk protocols on video, believing without sirens, risk-marker assessment, and a route to help the patient controls — with one honest limit stated up front (an unborn child engages safeguarding via the midwife, told to her, never behind her). Document securely; never send anything home. 0808 2000 247; 999 then 55 for silent calls.

knowledge.guideline: NICE PH50 (2014) domestic violence and abuse · NICE QS116 (2016) · NICE NG201 (2021) antenatal care · Domestic Abuse Act 2021
knowledge.summary: Headaches and tiredness can be the ticket to disclosure. Make it safe to talk, ask directly, believe, assess risk, and offer help the patient controls — with the honest limit that pregnancy brings.

points.t: On video or phone, confirm the patient is alone before asking about abuse, and agree a code phrase to end or switch the conversation. Never raise abuse if the partner may be present.

NICE PH50 and QS116: staff should be trained to ask about domestic abuse in a private discussion and respond appropriately. Clues here: repeated cancellations, an implausible injury explanation, long sleeves, control of her phone and money.
Non-fatal strangulation, escalation and pregnancy are high-risk markers on the SafeLives DASH risk checklist. Non-fatal strangulation is a specific offence under the Domestic Abuse Act 2021.

Offer IDVA referral with consent; National Domestic Abuse Helpline 0808 2000 247. High-risk cases go to MARAC. Antenatal booking with a midwife who knows; a pre-birth referral to children’s social care may be needed (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026).
Tension-type headache (NICE CG150): simple analgesia; in pregnancy paracetamol is preferred and NSAIDs are avoided, doses per BNF. Folic acid per BNF; book antenatal care promptly.
999, and 55 if unable to speak (Silent Solution). No letters, texts or calls to the home; secure, coded documentation; follow-up under a routine reason.

dg.d: Checked she was alone and safe to talk, agreed a code phrase, then an open question on the headaches.
Control of phone and money, isolation from her sister, pregnancy concealed from her partner.
No examination on video; in-person review under a routine pretext to document injuries and book antenatal care.
Tension-type headache confirmed; red-flag headache and head injury excluded; recognised the booking reason as a route to disclosure.
Identified strangulation, escalation and pregnancy as high-risk markers; checked tonight’s safety and obstetric symptoms.
Domestic abuse with high-risk features in early pregnancy; tension-type headache secondary to it.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: IDVA referral with consent, helpline stored safely, midwife booking with safeguarding awareness, MARAC considered, her pace respected.
Paracetamol for headache in pregnancy; folic acid and antenatal booking; emotional support.
999 and 55; maternity unit for pain or bleeding; disguised follow-up next week; secure documentation.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Sleeves in July, glances off-screen, “he doesn’t like me wasting doctors’ time”, the sideways baby question.
Idea (stress), concern (the baby, being reported and losing control), expectation (information without police).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she is 12 weeks pregnant by a violent partner who doesn’t know, and last month he held her by the throat. She’s terrified for the baby, terrified of being "reported" and losing control of what happens next, and using a headache appointment to test whether a doctor is safe — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Kayleigh, I’m Dr Lee — yes, it’s working, I can hear you fine. Before we start, is it all right to talk where you are? Is anyone else in the room or likely to walk in?
model.why: Checks it is safe to talk before anything else on video

model.text: (Glances off-screen.) Just me. Dean’s back soon though. He doesn’t like me wasting doctors’ time. It’s just headaches and I’m tired all the time.
You’re not wasting my time. If anyone comes in, say “about my prescription” and I’ll switch straight to headaches. You’re in charge of this call. Tell me about the headaches.
model.why: Agrees a code phrase and hands her control

model.text: Across my forehead, like a band. Months. Worse when things are tense at home.
Any headaches that wake you, come on suddenly and severely, or come with weakness, vision change or being sick? Any blow to the head?
model.why: Excludes headache red flags, including head injury

model.text: No, nothing like that.
You said it’s worse when things are tense at home. Can you tell me a bit about home?
model.why: Follows her own cue rather than a checklist

model.text: It’s… Dean likes things a certain way. He checks my phone, sorts the money. He doesn’t like my sister coming round.
Kayleigh, I ask lots of people this, and I’m asking because of what you’ve just said, not to catch you out. Are you ever frightened of Dean? Has he ever hurt you?
model.why: Asks directly and gently once it is safe

model.text: (Long pause.) He grabs me. Shakes me. Last month he held me against the wall. By my throat. He’s sorry after. It’s not all the time.
Thank you for telling me. I believe you. And none of this is your fault — none of it.
model.why: Believes out loud and removes blame

model.text: (Crying.) The door frame at A&E. That was him. And my arms — I’ve got marks under these sleeves.

I’m so sorry. I need to be honest about one thing: being held by the throat is the sign we take most seriously of all, because it’s the strongest warning that things can become very dangerous. It doesn’t mean police cars tonight. It means we plan properly now. Is it getting worse, or more often?
model.why: Names non-fatal strangulation as a high-risk marker and assesses escalation

model.text: It’s got worse this year. And… I’m pregnant. About twelve weeks. He doesn’t know. Is it true stress and being shaken about can hurt a baby?

That’s a really important question. The kindest true answer: the baby is most likely fine right now. The biggest risk to both of you isn’t stress — it’s this carrying on, because it often gets worse in pregnancy. Any tummy pain or bleeding since?
model.why: Answers the question she came with honestly, and checks obstetric symptoms

model.text: No. No bleeding.
Is it safe for you to be at home tonight? If it wasn’t, where could you go?
I think tonight’s okay. My sister in Chesterfield. She’d have me. I just don’t want police at the door. I don’t want it all taken out of my hands.

You stay in control of the speed. There are specialist domestic abuse workers called IDVAs who help women plan safely — would you let me refer you? And there’s a 24-hour helpline, 0808 2000 247. Save it in your phone under a different name, like a hair salon.
model.why: Offers IDVA referral and helpline with safe storage

model.text: Salon. Okay. Yes, you can refer me, if they don’t ring the house.

I’ll make sure they use a safe number and times you choose. One honest thing, so there are no surprises: because you’re pregnant, the midwife needs to know about this so she can support you both. I’ll tell you before anything is shared, never behind your back. Is that all right?
model.why: States the honest limit on confidentiality in advance

model.text: If it helps the baby. Yes.

Here’s the plan that leaves no trace. I’ll book you in next week for “pregnancy bloods” — that’s our next talk, in person, alone, and I can look at your arms then. Nothing gets posted or texted to you. If you’re ever in danger: 999. If you can’t speak, press 55 when they answer. Tummy pain or bleeding — contact the maternity unit the same day.
model.why: Disguised follow-up, silent-call advice and obstetric safety-net

model.text: Pregnancy bloods. He’d not question that.
Just so I know it’s clear — what will you do if things get dangerous before next week?
999, and 55 if I can’t talk. Or get to my sister. And the salon number.
Exactly. You did something brave today. I’ll record this securely so no one rings the house.
model.why: Closes warmly and confirms secure documentation

social.t: Phone checking, controlling money and isolating her from her sister are coercive control, a criminal offence (Serious Crime Act 2015, s76). Economic abuse limits her ability to leave.
Abuse often starts or escalates in pregnancy. Midwives ask about domestic abuse at booking (NICE NG201, 2021); women with complex social factors need tailored antenatal care (NICE CG110, 2010).

legal.t: Statutory definition includes physical, emotional, economic abuse and controlling behaviour. The Act created a specific offence of non-fatal strangulation.

An adult with capacity decides about police involvement. Disclosure without consent can be justified to prevent serious harm or where a child is at risk — tell her first where safe (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
Where there is risk to an unborn baby, a pre-birth referral to children’s social care may be needed (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026). Explain this to her before it happens.

professional.t: Use the SafeLives DASH risk checklist; strangulation, escalation and pregnancy are high-risk markers. High-risk cases go to MARAC, and information can be shared without consent where risk is high — tell her if this is planned.
Code the record, restrict online record access for third-party and sensitive entries, and flag that the practice must not phone the home or send letters (NICE PH50, 2014).

community.t: National Domestic Abuse Helpline 0808 2000 247 (24 hours); IDVA services; refuges; Silent Solution (999 then 55 on a mobile); the Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme (Clare’s Law).

redFlags: Non-fatal strangulation (held by the throat) — strongest single risk marker
Escalation in frequency or severity, especially since pregnancy
Pregnancy with abdominal pain or bleeding after assault — same-day maternity assessment
psychosocial: Control of phone and money; isolation from her sister
Fear of police involvement and losing control
ice: Concern: the baby, and being reported without her say
Expectation: information and a route to help she controls, with nothing he can find

playbook.diagnosis: Domestic abuse with high-risk features (non-fatal strangulation, escalation, pregnancy) presenting as tension-type headache and tiredness in a woman about 12 weeks pregnant.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “What you’re describing is domestic abuse. The headaches are real, and they’re linked to what’s happening at home. Being held by the throat is the warning sign we take most seriously, so let’s plan to keep you and the baby safe.”

management.reflectIce: “You came to find out if the baby is all right and whether you can get help without police at the door. The baby is most likely fine, and yes — there’s help you control.”
management.psychosocial: Her pace, her controls: IDVA referral with consent, the sister as a safe place, helpline disguised in her phone, and a follow-up he has no reason to question.
sharedPlan: IDVA referral with consent; DASH risk assessment; MARAC if high risk, telling her first
Antenatal booking with a midwife, sharing the concern so she and the baby are supported
In-person review next week under a routine reason to document injuries
safetyNet: 999 if in danger; press 55 if unable to speak
Abdominal pain or bleeding — same-day maternity assessment; nothing posted, texted or phoned home

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by consulting on the headache the patient booked, not the danger she is in — or by rescuing her too fast. Safety to talk, belief, risk markers and her control are what score.

items.fail: Asking about abuse before checking she is alone on the video call.
items.why: Unsafe practice; if the partner overhears, her risk rises immediately.
items.fix: “Before anything else — are you alone? If someone comes in, say ‘my prescription’.”

items.fail: Missing or minimising “held by the throat”.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious risk.” Non-fatal strangulation is a high-risk marker.
items.fix: Name it: “That’s the sign we take most seriously of all.” Then ask about escalation and pregnancy.

items.fail: “Why do you stay?” or “You need to leave him.”
items.fix: “I believe you. None of this is your fault.” Then plan at her pace.

items.fail: Promising total confidentiality, or sharing with the midwife without telling her.
items.why: Both break trust; the unborn baby means information will be shared.
items.fix: State the limit before it applies: “The midwife needs to know, and I’ll tell you before anything is shared.”

items.fail: Texting the helpline number or posting a leaflet home.
items.why: Creates evidence the abuser can find.
items.fix: Save the number under a disguised name during the call; follow up under a routine reason.

items.fail: No emergency plan before the call ends.
items.why: Safety-netting inadequate for a high-risk situation.
items.fix: 999, 55 if she can’t speak, the sister as a safe place, maternity unit for pain or bleeding — then teach-back.

timeMap.d: Before any history: alone? likely interruptions? agree a code phrase. On video the room itself may not be safe.
Brief headache red flags, then follow “worse when things are tense at home”. Ask directly and gently about fear and harm.
“I believe you. It’s not your fault.” Name strangulation as high risk, ask about escalation, answer the baby question honestly.
Tonight’s safety, the sister, IDVA referral, helpline saved under a disguise, midwife and the honest limit on confidentiality.
999 and 55; maternity unit for pain or bleeding; “pregnancy bloods” next week; secure records. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Treats the headache and ends the call; never asks about home; asks “why don’t you leave?”; promises total confidentiality; sends a text or letter home; misses the pregnancy.
wordPics.pass: Checks she is alone, asks directly about abuse, believes her, recognises the strangulation risk, offers the helpline and IDVA referral, arranges follow-up and safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: code phrase before any history; names strangulation, escalation and pregnancy as a high-risk cluster; answers the baby question honestly; states the midwife limit in advance; builds a disguised, no-trace follow-up and 55 silent-call advice; she leaves feeling in control.

avoid.instead: “I believe you, and none of this is your fault. Let’s plan what keeps you safe, at your pace.”
avoid.why: Blames the victim and ignores that leaving is often the most dangerous time.

avoid.dont: “Everything you tell me is completely confidential.”
avoid.instead: “Mostly, yes — but because you’re pregnant the midwife needs to know, and I’ll tell you before anything is shared.”
avoid.why: A promise you can’t keep destroys trust when it is broken.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send you a text with some useful numbers.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s save the helpline in your phone as a hair salon, right now.”
avoid.why: Anything he can find increases her risk.

Tension-type headache confirmed; red-flag headache and head injury excluded; recognised the booking reason as a route to disclosure.
Identified strangulation, escalation and pregnancy as high-risk markers; checked tonight’s safety and obstetric symptoms.
Domestic abuse with high-risk features in early pregnancy; tension-type headache secondary to it.
IDVA referral with consent, helpline stored safely, midwife booking with safeguarding awareness, MARAC considered, her pace respected.
Paracetamol for headache in pregnancy; folic acid and antenatal booking; emotional support.
999 and 55; maternity unit for pain or bleeding; disguised follow-up next week; secure documentation.

social.t: Phone checking, controlling money and isolating her from her sister are coercive control, a criminal offence (Serious Crime Act 2015, s76). Economic abuse limits her ability to leave.
Abuse often starts or escalates in pregnancy. Midwives ask about domestic abuse at booking (NICE NG201, 2021); women with complex social factors need tailored antenatal care (NICE CG110, 2010).

legal.t: Statutory definition includes physical, emotional, economic abuse and controlling behaviour. The Act created a specific offence of non-fatal strangulation.

An adult with capacity decides about police involvement. Disclosure without consent can be justified to prevent serious harm or where a child is at risk — tell her first where safe (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
Where there is risk to an unborn baby, a pre-birth referral to children’s social care may be needed (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026). Explain this to her before it happens.

professional.t: Use the SafeLives DASH risk checklist; strangulation, escalation and pregnancy are high-risk markers. High-risk cases go to MARAC, and information can be shared without consent where risk is high — tell her if this is planned.
Code the record, restrict online record access for third-party and sensitive entries, and flag that the practice must not phone the home or send letters (NICE PH50, 2014).

community.t: National Domestic Abuse Helpline 0808 2000 247 (24 hours); IDVA services; refuges; Silent Solution (999 then 55 on a mobile); the Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme (Clare’s Law).

redFlags: Non-fatal strangulation (held by the throat) — strongest single risk marker
Escalation in frequency or severity, especially since pregnancy
Pregnancy with abdominal pain or bleeding after assault — same-day maternity assessment
psychosocial: Control of phone and money; isolation from her sister
Fear of police involvement and losing control
ice: Concern: the baby, and being reported without her say
Expectation: information and a route to help she controls, with nothing he can find

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Domestic abuse with high-risk features (non-fatal strangulation, escalation, pregnancy) presenting as tension-type headache and tiredness in a woman about 12 weeks pregnant.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “What you’re describing is domestic abuse. The headaches are real, and they’re linked to what’s happening at home. Being held by the throat is the warning sign we take most seriously, so let’s plan to keep you and the baby safe.”

management.reflectIce: “You came to find out if the baby is all right and whether you can get help without police at the door. The baby is most likely fine, and yes — there’s help you control.”
management.psychosocial: Her pace, her controls: IDVA referral with consent, the sister as a safe place, helpline disguised in her phone, and a follow-up he has no reason to question.
sharedPlan: IDVA referral with consent; DASH risk assessment; MARAC if high risk, telling her first
Antenatal booking with a midwife, sharing the concern so she and the baby are supported
In-person review next week under a routine reason to document injuries
safetyNet: 999 if in danger; press 55 if unable to speak
Abdominal pain or bleeding — same-day maternity assessment; nothing posted, texted or phoned home

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by consulting on the headache the patient booked, not the danger she is in — or by rescuing her too fast. Safety to talk, belief, risk markers and her control are what score.

items.fail: Asking about abuse before checking she is alone on the video call.
items.why: Unsafe practice; if the partner overhears, her risk rises immediately.
items.fix: “Before anything else — are you alone? If someone comes in, say ‘my prescription’.”

items.fail: Missing or minimising “held by the throat”.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious risk.” Non-fatal strangulation is a high-risk marker.
items.fix: Name it: “That’s the sign we take most seriously of all.” Then ask about escalation and pregnancy.

items.fail: “Why do you stay?” or “You need to leave him.”
items.fix: “I believe you. None of this is your fault.” Then plan at her pace.

items.fail: Promising total confidentiality, or sharing with the midwife without telling her.
items.why: Both break trust; the unborn baby means information will be shared.
items.fix: State the limit before it applies: “The midwife needs to know, and I’ll tell you before anything is shared.”

items.fail: Texting the helpline number or posting a leaflet home.
items.why: Creates evidence the abuser can find.
items.fix: Save the number under a disguised name during the call; follow up under a routine reason.

items.fail: No emergency plan before the call ends.
items.why: Safety-netting inadequate for a high-risk situation.
items.fix: 999, 55 if she can’t speak, the sister as a safe place, maternity unit for pain or bleeding — then teach-back.
